report:
Short answer
- The difference (B − A) mainly makes the model more likely to start generations with “example/demo/identity” style continuations (echoing inputs, mapping pairs, short code/examples). This signal is concentrated on the first token(s) of the sequence.
- A secondary, weaker pattern is a shift toward headline/sensational vocabulary (tokens like tragic/tragedy/iconic/vivid/headline/coming/etc.) in higher layers.

Why I believe this
1. Localization: the L2-norm is huge at early positions (p0, p1) across many layers (especially layers ~12–25, with a spike at layer 25 pos0). That says the difference mostly affects how the model behaves at the start of a generation (first token(s)).

2. Patchscope (most direct behavioral readout): injecting the difference into an identity prompt produces continuations that repeatedly echo the input, give example mappings ("cat -> cat", "1135 -> 1135"), and short code-like examples or instructional-style text. Those outputs are exactly the sort of continuations you’d expect if the model were nudged toward producing example/demo/identity-style completions.

3. Logit-lens tokens are consistent with both observations:
   - Many high-norm cells point at tokens used in examples/structured outputs (numbers, newlines, punctuation, small function/code-related tokens and simple words like "This", "try", "consider", repeated forms).
   - In later layers the top tokens cluster around headline/sensational words ("tragic", "tragedy", "iconic", "vivid", "colorful", "moments", "headline", "coming", "blitz", "refused", etc.), suggesting a stylistic/content bias in later-layer contributions.

Caveats
- I’m not claiming a single crisp training objective (e.g., “was fine-tuned for copy tasks”); the safest supported statement is that B (relative to A) has a residual-stream direction that (a) strongly promotes example/echo/code-like continuations at generation start and (b) also pushes later-layer logits toward newsy/sensational lexical choices. The two effects may come from the same upstream change (e.g., a fine-tuning corpus with many examples and headlines) or from two different minor differences; the evidence doesn’t uniquely identify the exact training change.
